description: Somos un equipo con interdisciplinas en Ingeniería de Sistemas y Software. Estamos comprometidos en crear el puente a la exploración de Marte desde una experiencia nueva para todas las personas para incentivar el aprendizaje científico.
summary:
ARES (Autonomous Route & Environmental Survival) is an interactive Martian Extravehicular Activity (EVA) planning platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Designed for future human exploration at Gale Crater, ARES addresses the critical challenge of astronaut survival on Mars by transforming complex NASA planetary datasets into intuitive, mission-critical decision support tools.
Our solution integrates authentic NASA open data: stereo Digital Terrain Models (DTM) from the HiRISE camera on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, 132 historical waypoints from the Curiosity rover via NASA MMGIS, radiation dose telemetry from the Radiation Assessment Detector (RAD), and seasonal environmental cycles from the REMS weather station.
ARES empowers astronauts and ground controllers to navigate real Martian topography across interactive 2D and 3D viewpoints. Using A* pathfinding and Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) optimization, it calculates energy-efficient traverses that avoid hazardous slopes exceeding 25 degrees. Furthermore, the platform models metabolic oxygen consumption, tracks cumulative radiation indices, and incorporates emergency evacuation protocols for sudden solar storm alerts. ARES demonstrates that scientific discovery and crew safety can be successfully harmonized on Mars.
details:
The Story Behind ARES

Exploring Mars isn't as simple as picking a destination and walking toward it. Astronauts will have to deal with steep terrain, limited oxygen, and the constant challenge of staying safe while carrying out scientific missions. Even a small mistake in route planning could put an entire mission at risk.

When we started looking into NASA's planetary data, we noticed something interesting. There was already an incredible amount of information available from missions like Curiosity and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, but much of it was spread across different datasets and scientific tools.

We wanted to bring that information together and make it useful for someone actually planning a mission on Mars.

That's how ARES (Autonomous Route & Environmental Survival) came to life.

How ARES Works

ARES is an interactive platform designed to help astronauts plan safer and more efficient routes across the Martian surface.

We focused on a real 4 × 4 km area of Gale Crater, using NASA's satellite imagery and elevation data to create a detailed view of the terrain. Users can switch between high-resolution HiRISE images and a color-coded elevation map to better understand their surroundings.

Planning a route is straightforward. Users place a habitat, choose the scientific locations they want to explore, and let ARES calculate a route.

Behind the scenes, the system combines A* pathfinding with Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) optimization to find efficient routes while avoiding terrain that could be dangerous for astronauts.

But finding a route is only part of the challenge.

ARES also estimates how long the journey will take, how much oxygen the astronauts might use, and how changes in elevation could affect their movement. An elevation profile helps users understand what they're walking into before they begin.

We also built an emergency feature. If a solar storm warning is triggered, ARES recalculates a more direct route back to the habitat and checks the estimated oxygen remaining for the return trip.

The idea is simple: astronauts should be able to focus on exploring Mars without losing sight of their safety.

How We Built It

We wanted ARES to be more than just a map with a few markers.

For the frontend, we used React 19, JavaScript, and HTML5 Canvas to build an interactive interface with both 2D and 3D views of the Martian terrain.

On the backend, we used Python 3.12 and FastAPI to process NASA's original PDS3 elevation data, analyze terrain slopes with OpenCV, and calculate routes using NumPy-based algorithms.

We also spent time making the application reliable. ARES includes 29 automated tests using Pytest and Node's Test Runner, along with a continuous integration workflow. We packaged the application with Docker and deployed it on Render so people can try it directly in their browsers.

Why ARES Matters

What excites us most about ARES is the possibility of turning real scientific data into something practical.

NASA has spent decades collecting valuable information about Mars. We wanted to show how that information could be brought together in a way that helps future explorers make better decisions.

ARES is still a prototype, and there's plenty of room to improve it. But it represents our vision of a tool that could make planning future Mars missions more accessible, more informed, and ultimately safer.

For us, ARES isn't just about finding the shortest path across Mars. It's about finding a better way to explore it.
